title: Theories of the Firm: The Resource-Based View, VRIO or VRIN
keyQuestion: What is a firm? Why does it exist? Does AI offer a firm a sustainable competitive advantage?

reading.name: The Resource-Based View: VRIO or VRIN (VRIO Brief)

case.name: VRIO Assignment: Diagnosing a Firm's Competitive Position (your team: In-N-Out)

slides: S6 slides (29): profit pools, how much industry matters, TCE, knowledge-based view, resource categories, VRIO table, BYU VRIO exercise

framework.name: VRIO as a sequential gate
framework.summary: Two firms facing the same customers, suppliers and regulation still out-earn one another because they are not resource-equivalent. The RBV rests on two assumptions: resources are heterogeneous and imperfectly mobile. VRIO asks four sequential yes/no questions about ONE resource or capability; the first 'no' stops the analysis and fixes the verdict. Its value is that it disqualifies most strengths.

components.name: Valuable
components.what: Does it let the firm exploit an opportunity or neutralize a threat by raising WTP or lowering cost? Practical: if it disappeared tomorrow, would revenue fall or cost rise?

components.name: Rare
components.what: Controlled by only a small number of competitors? If every serious rival has it, it is a requirement to compete, not a source of advantage.

components.name: Costly to imitate
components.what: Is it costly or difficult for firms that lack it to acquire or develop it? Could a well-funded rival get it, and how long would that take? This is where most advantages die.

components.name: Organized
components.what: Is the firm structured, incentivized and staffed to capture the value? Organization converts potential into captured earnings.

components.name: Four barriers to imitation
components.what: Unique history / path dependence (built under conditions that no longer exist); causal ambiguity (even insiders can't specify why it works); social complexity (rooted in relationships, trust, norms); legal and economic deterrents (patents and exclusive contracts make imitation unlawful; scale, switching costs and network effects make it uneconomic — NVIDIA's 7.5M CUDA developers).

components.name: Verdict table (brief / Canvas)
components.what: V=No → competitive disadvantage; V yes, R no → parity ('a requirement to compete'); V, R yes, I no → temporary advantage; V, R, I yes, O no → unexploited advantage ('value left on the table'); all yes → sustained advantage.

components.name: Verdict table (S6 slides version, labeled)
components.what: The slides use an older five-row table: failure (N,N,N,N), parity (Y,N,N,N), competitive advantage (Y,Y,N,N), durable competitive advantage (Y,Y,Y,N), sustained competitive advantage (Y,Y,Y,Y), with 'Is the resource imitable?' as the column. Teach the brief's version as primary; recognize the slide labels if they appear.

components.name: Resources vs. capabilities
components.what: Resources are stocks the firm owns or controls (tangible: cash, real estate, branches, plants, spectrum, patents; intangible: brand, reputation, culture, relationships). Capabilities are flows — what the firm is repeatedly good at, embedded in routines. Capabilities are often more defensible: you can buy a building, not fifteen years of underwriting judgment.

components.name: VRIN and the lineage
components.what: VRIN (valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable, non-substitutable) is the earlier formulation. VRIO folds non-substitutability into imitability (a substitute is another path to imitating the benefit) and adds Organization. Still name substitutes explicitly: substitution most often ends an advantage imitation could not touch.

terms.def: The view that persistent differences in returns between firms facing the same environment come from differences in what they control.
Firms hold different bundles of resources.
Bundles cannot be bought, copied or rebuilt quickly. If either assumption fails, returns converge.
An asset the firm owns or controls; a stock (tangible or intangible). Slides: four categories — physical, financial, human, intangible.
What a firm is repeatedly good at doing; a flow embedded in organizational routines that deploy resources.
Valuable but not rare: competence sustains parity and nothing more (regional bank branches).
Valuable and rare but not costly to imitate.
Valuable, rare, costly to imitate, but the firm is not organized to capture it — often the most actionable case because the constraint is internal (Intel).
Passes all four tests (Visa). Substitution check keeps 'sustained' from meaning 'permanent'.
A resource built under conditions that no longer exist; money can buy the same category of asset today but not the same asset.
Even insiders can't fully specify why a capability works, so outsiders can't copy the recipe.
Rooted in relationships, trust and norms among many people; can be described but not engineered on demand or bought as a unit.
Analysis of a firm's resources and capabilities to assess how effectively it can deliver the unique value it hopes to provide.
Williamson (Nobel 2009): the analysis of economic governance, especially the boundaries of the firm — firms exist where organizing a transaction internally is cheaper than using the market.
Firm boundaries surround critical knowledge elements (Chick-fil-A: sauce, cooking chicken, in-store operations, training inside; raising chickens, making cups/forks, making soda outside).

claims.claim: The practical value of VRIO is not that it identifies strengths — every team can list strengths — but that it disqualifies most of them and forces attention onto the few assets actually carrying the position.
Value and rarity are the easy tests; nearly every diagnosis turns on imitability.
An asset can be expensive, hard-won and operationally excellent and still be nothing more than a requirement to compete (branch networks).
Organization is the mechanism that converts potential into captured earnings; fix the fourth test and the same resources begin to earn (Intel's Q2 2026 recovery).
Buying a rare resource and being organized to exploit it are separate achievements, and only the second pays (Capital One / Discover).

Business-unit effects explain 3-5x as much profit variance as industry effects; every study since Schmalensee finds the same ordering (e.g., McGahan & Porter 1997: industry 18.7%, corporate 4.3%, business unit 31.5%).
Most resources are parity; a page of 'yes' answers usually means the tests were not applied.

failures.name: Generic strengths
failures.what: 'Data' is not a resource; 'proprietary risk-pricing data drawn from forty years of claims' is.

failures.name: Conflating valuable with popular, rare with impressive
failures.what: Rubric warns against it; rarity must be judged against named competitors.

failures.name: Not stopping at the first no
failures.what: Leave later columns blank once a test returns no; the verdict is fixed.

failures.name: No time-to-imitate
failures.what: Imitability should name the blocking mechanism AND estimate how long a funded rival would take.

failures.name: Undated verdicts
failures.what: VRIO is a snapshot; note where a verdict is fragile, what would break it and how soon.

caseFacts.fact: Visa: four-party network, ~5B credentials, 175M+ merchant locations, 258B transactions, $40.0B net revenue (+11%), ~60% operating margin; Mastercard $32.8B at 57.6%. V/R/I/O all yes → sustained; exposure is substitution (Pix 79.8B transactions; UPI 23.66B in July 2026) and interchange regulation (June 2026 settlement).
caseFacts.why: Model of a sustained advantage plus the substitution check.

caseFacts.fact: Regional bank branches: valuable (FDIC avg savings 0.38% vs. online >4%), not rare → parity. Branch openings exceeded closings three straight quarters into Q2 2026; the asset is being repositioned to advice and acquisition.
caseFacts.why: Model of parity — and how a verdict's activity can change while the verdict holds.

caseFacts.fact: McKinsey: reputation + 50,000-alumni network pass V, R, I; organization '?' — $600M (2021) and $650M (Dec 2024) settlements, frozen starting salaries, headcount ~40,000 (down >10%), revenue flat ~$15-16B vs. Deloitte $70.5B.
caseFacts.why: Model of an Organization question (the up-or-out pyramid under strain from cost and AI).

caseFacts.fact: Intel: leading-edge fabs + x86 are V, R, I but O = no: 2024 net loss $18.8B; foundry operating losses $13.3B (2024) and $10.3B (2025) = $23.6B; US government took 9.9% for $8.9B. Q2 2026 under new CEO: revenue $16.1B (+25%), operating income $1.8B.
caseFacts.why: Model of an unexploited advantage — 'the resource was never the binding constraint; the organization was.'

caseFacts.fact: Your team's In-N-Out paper: cult brand, private ownership, vertically integrated supply chain (Lancaster, TX plant; one-day-drive radius), employee model all rated sustained; menu simplicity parity; geographic restraint temporary.
caseFacts.why: Calibration: four of six all-yes is what the assignment warns about; employee model rarity is weak (rivals copy parts — Chipotle promotes 85% of managers from within); no time-to-imitate estimates.

strongAnalysis: What is a firm and why does it exist? TCE: firms exist where internal governance beats market transactions (boundaries of the firm). Knowledge-based view: boundaries surround critical knowledge. RBV: a firm is a bundle of heterogeneous, imperfectly mobile resources and capabilities; that bundle — not the industry — explains most of the persistent variance in returns (business unit 3-5x industry).

Does AI offer a sustainable advantage? Run VRIO on 'AI': valuable yes; rare — not when frontier models are available to every rival via API; costly to imitate — no for generic capability. So generic AI is parity at best, temporary if early. AI contributes to sustained advantage only when bundled with a resource that IS rare and hard to copy (proprietary data accumulated over time — path dependence; workflow integration and switching costs; organizational routines that are socially complex) and when the firm is organized to exploit it. (Application of the VRIO brief; the brief doesn't answer this directly.)
Also note AI as a threat to Organization: the McKinsey case — AI pressure on the base of the pyramid that appropriates the value of reputation.
Method discipline: one resource at a time; stop at the first no; name competitors for rarity; name the barrier and time to imitate; check substitutes; date the verdict.

counter.argument: VRIO is static and tautological: 'valuable' resources are identified by the fact the firm is successful, so it explains success after the fact.
counter.response: The brief anticipates this by making each test operational (if it disappeared, would revenue fall or cost rise; name competitors for rarity; estimate time to imitate) and by dating every verdict. Used as a gate on one resource at a time, it mostly says 'no' — that is its value. The substitution check and the 'verdicts move' examples (branches, Intel) make it dynamic.

courseMap.text: After the outward look (PEST, Five Forces), the RBV asks what the firm brings. VRIO's imitability barriers recur in differentiation durability (S9: path dependence, causal ambiguity, social complexity, credible commitment) and in cost advantages (structure that rivals cannot copy piecemeal, S1/S7).

slideExtras.detail: Schmalensee 1985 industry 19.5%, business unit 0.6%; Rumelt 1991 8.3% / 2.0% corporate / 46.3% BU; Roquebert 1996 10.2 / 17.9 / 37.1; McGahan & Porter 1997 18.7 / 4.3 / 31.5; Misangyi 2006 7.6 / 7.2 / 36.4; Vanneste 2017 meta 8.0 / 14.0 / 36.0. 'The business unit runs three to five times industry.'

PC industry: manufacturers compete in the largest but least-profitable segment; microprocessors and software earn the margins. Fitness industry: live classes/subscriptions and supplements vs. gym memberships.

Physical: bank branches (JPMorgan 5,292), oil reserves (Aramco 259B). Financial: Berkshire $344B cash. Human: best places to work. Intangible: patent owners (Samsung, LG, TSMC...), most admired companies.
Buildings, location, support from the church, faculty working for less than market, culture — run through V, R, I, O.
Story of the 61-year-old farmer who won the Sydney-Melbourne ultramarathon by shuffling through the night: a sustainable, unconventional approach; character and competence.

S6 slides' VRIO table conflicts with the brief's; both shown and labeled.
